caption:
PewDiePie is training his own AI model. OpenAI banned him twice.
Here's why that matters more than the drama.

The most personal software you'll ever use isn't yours. It reads your email, sits in your calendar, watches your browsing. And the company that owns it also owns everything it learns about you.
Odysseus is his answer. Free, open source, self-hosted. An AI assistant running on your own machine for browsing, email, calendar and tasks, with nothing going to Big Tech.
The weak point was the models. People were plugging in general chat models, built to talk rather than to actually do everyday work.

So he started training his own, called Ajax.
Getting training data was the hard part. Odysseus doesn't collect chats, so he asked people to donate theirs and built a site for it. Nobody submitted anything. He then tried generating examples with OpenAI, which is where the bans came in: twice for distillation, restored on appeal, then banned again.

That's his account, and training on a competitor's outputs does break OpenAI's terms. It's a genuine constraint on open models, not just a good story.

The design choices are the interesting part:
- Ajax is a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-9B, built for the tools inside Odysseus
- he wanted something far bigger, then realised almost nobody could run it at home
- so he went smaller on purpose, aimed at browsing, email and calendars
- he used Heretic to strip the constant refusals on ordinary work

He plans to open-source it. That's the whole point.
Because if your assistant is closed, your most personal data trains their model, their model sets your price, and you end up renting access to your own life.
